newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. not ready to lift sanctions on China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. not ready to lift sanctions on China.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Saturday that Washington was not yet ready to lift sanctions on China though it would continue to consider the issue.

The United States imposed sanctions on Beijing after the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown on democracy activists but though it has since lifted some, others, like a ban on military sales, are still in place.
Ahead of a U.S.-China summit on Sunday that is expected to herald a new era of bilateral cooperation, Christopher said:
"We would like to reach the point where we felt there was justification for dropping the 1989 sanctions but we're not there yet. We'll continue to review the matter."

On another sensitive topic -- China's arms and nuclear trade with Iran -- Foreign Minister Qian Qichen seemed to deny a published report that Beijing recently made sales that may violate its international commitments or U.S. laws.

Referring to a Washington Times story about Central Intelligence Agency findings that China recently sold Iran missile technology, advanced radar components and nearly 400 tons of chemicals used to produce nerve agents, Qian said:
"That newspe Asia Pacific Economic forum. APEC heads of state hold a summit on Monday.
Christopher's visit to Beijing earlier this week -- his first in more than two years -- solidified a new basis for strategic cooperation between China and the United States.
After Tiananmen Square, the two countries were locked in a confrontational and mistrustful relationship that now shows signs of marked improvement.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin are to reinforce that progress when they meet in Manila.

The two leaders have been expected to announce specific dates, or at least a timetable, for an exchange of summits in each other's capital. But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said this "may or may not happen."
Qian, without giving details, predicted the Sunday meeting would be successful.

Christopher stressed that "confrontation and containment are not the direction the United States is going with respect to China. We think that would be self-defeating for the United States and the world."

Instead, he said: "We want to emphasise the importance of cooperating and working together on many issues on which we have common interest and finding ways to manage those issues on which we have differences."
Apart from sanctions, another, even bigger, difference has to do with China's arms and nuclear trade with Iran.

Quoting an Oct 2 CIA report, the Washignton Times this week said the alleged recent transfer of missile-guidance components to Iran may violate Beijing's 1994 commitment to an international pact curbing such sales.
Alleged recent arms-technology transfers may violate a 1992 U.S. law requiring sanctions to be imposed on nations exporting destabilising conventional weapons to Iran or Iraq, it added.
Christopher reiterated general U.S. concerns about trade with Iran, which Washington considers a sponsor of terrorism.. He said he had urged the Chinese "not to be involved in that kind of trade."

China assured the United States it was abiding by its commitments. But Christopher added: "It is our obligation to try to ensure our information is up to date on this subject and we will certainly bring it to their attention as we develop information that might be inconsistent with their prior commitments."
Christopher's spokesman said on Friday there was no question China continued to have trade with Iran and promised the new CIA charges against Beijing would be looked into.
But the spokesman also said there was no proof to date that China was guilty of violations and the charges would not derail a planned exchange of summits in Washington and Beijing.
